text:
Sampled-candidate and full-catalog metrics can disagree on model ordering, so diagnostic gains need empirical validation. Foundational work shows sampled ranking metrics can reverse comparisons even in expectation ([Krichene and Rendle](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651)); RecSys 2025 revisits sampling reliability ([On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). A 2024 study demonstrates benefits from correcting sampled rank estimates when training WARP/LambdaRank, providing an actionable loss-ablation hypothesis, but no guarantee for SASRec or this benchmark ([Subbiah et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06371)). Temporal leakage and negative sampling are established evaluation hazards ([Hidasi and Czapp](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/eval_flaws_recsys23.pdf)). These findings support testing diagnostic usefulness; they do not establish it for the four Amazon categories.

Suggested experiment: create auxiliary temporal holdouts exclusively within training histories; fit diagnostic models on earlier prefixes, excluding held-out interactions from every learned statistic. On identical users/targets, compare fixed 99-unique-negative HR@10 with full-catalog unseen-item HR@10/NDCG@10, retaining the target and documenting item availability. Track model-order agreement and whether diagnostic changes predict gains from targeted, retrained component ablations—such as sampling correction or removal of sequence modeling. Use paired user bootstrap intervals within each category, then average the four resampled category scores equally; report category effects and macro differences. User bootstrap captures user-sampling uncertainty, not training-seed variability or generalization beyond these four datasets. Treat this as a proposed validation design. Keep host selection exclusively on pinned macro validation HR@10: 200 users/category, 99 unique negatives, seed 42; auxiliary diagnostics and twenty-user recommendation lists remain explanatory evidence.
